ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations, including frequent greetings, side chatter, and occasional technical check-ins. Speakers use many fillers and repairs—“um,” “yeah,” repeated words, false starts, and self-corrections—especially when thinking aloud or navigating transitions. The presentations are long, structured monologues with informal spoken signposting (“all right,” “so,” “okay”) and repeated emphasis on what the audience should notice; audience questions tend to be prefaced with praise, disclaimers such as “quick” or “naive” question, and several clauses of setup before the question itself. Overlap is modest but common at turn boundaries, with brief acknowledgments, laughter-like reactions, and supportive interjections. Participants challenge ideas indirectly and politely, framing alternatives as curiosities or open questions rather than contradictions. The overall register is professionally technical but socially relaxed, with frequent appreciation, collaborative invitations, and conversational follow-ups rather than rigid moderation.

Meeting style for this meeting (screen_share_working_session): Someone is sharing a document, figure or spreadsheet and the group works through it. People point at what is on screen ('that column', 'the second figure'), but whoever is reading still says the key numbers, names and dates out loud, since only the audio is recorded. Turns are short and practical, with pauses while someone scrolls or reads.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Can you scroll up- no, further. Yeah, that row.
  - That one's wrong, I think. Or it's from the old file.
  - Hang on, let me find it. Okay, give me a sec.
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Choosing which retrofits to fund so older apartment buildings stay safe during multi-day heat waves.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a postdoctoral researcher with 6 years of experience studying overheating in older multifamily housing. Her work combines building-energy simulation, field monitoring with indoor temperature and humidity sensors, and feeder-level load estimation during extreme-heat events. She has worked with naturally ventilated prewar and mid-century apartment buildings and is attentive to the practical limits imposed by aging electrical service, tenant behavior, and incomplete building records.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya frames the retrofit decision as a coupled physical-systems problem: the building envelope, solar gains, internal heat, occupant window use, cooling equipment, and local electric distribution system interact over several consecutive hot nights. She wants comparable building inputs and clearly specified heat-wave scenarios before making health or cost claims, and is wary of relying on self-reported comfort or broad citywide averages as substitutes for measured or modeled indoor exposure.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Alvarez
speakers.background: Dr. Alvarez is a public-health project manager with 12 years of experience coordinating municipal heat-response evaluations, syndromic-surveillance analyses, and community-based studies of medically vulnerable residents. He has worked with emergency-department visit data, cooling-center attendance records, mortality surveillance, and neighborhood vulnerability indices, including the governance restrictions that shape access to health data. His recent work has focused on the unequal burden of heat exposure among older adults, people with cardiopulmonary disease, and residents with limited mobility.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis treats a safe indoor temperature as an important but incomplete outcome. He focuses on exposure, susceptibility, access to alternatives such as cooling centers, and the pathways through which heat becomes illness or an emergency visit. He will press the group to define clinically meaningful outcomes and equity-relevant subgroups, while acknowledging uncertainty about how to translate building-level temperature reductions into attributable health effects when available surveillance measures are aggregate and imperfect.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Priya Shah
speakers.background: Priya Shah is a fourth-year economics PhD student studying housing, energy affordability, and landlord-tenant incentives. She has experience assembling property-level administrative data, estimating household electricity-bill burdens, and conducting semi-structured interviews with affordable-housing owners and tenant advocates. Her dissertation examines how split incentives and financing constraints affect adoption of energy and resilience upgrades in rental housing.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya views retrofit choice as a distributional and incentive problem, not simply a ranking of engineering performance. She wants to distinguish who pays the upfront capital cost from who receives lower bills, improved comfort, and avoided health risk. She is interested in transparent comparisons across measures, sensitivity analysis for uncertain utilization and electricity prices, and pilot rules that do not unintentionally favor owners who can already finance upgrades or burden tenants with higher operating costs.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a practical planning meeting among Dr. Maya Chen (environmental engineering), Dr. Luis Alvarez (public health), and Priya Shah (economics). They should discuss how to form an evidence plan for prioritizing heat-safety retrofits in older apartment buildings. Near the end, the group must explicitly settle on exactly six action items. Include these six items and no additional action items: (1) Maya Chen will prepare a preliminary indoor-temperature and grid-load modeling scope by June 14, 2027; (2) Luis Alvarez will provide available aggregate heat-related emergency-visit and cooling-center-use measures, including their limitations, by June 21, 2027; (3) Priya Shah will draft a framework for comparing landlord capital costs with tenant electricity-bill impacts by June 18, 2027; (4) obtain a current list of potentially eligible older apartment buildings; (5) identify which tenant and landlord consent or data-sharing steps are required; and (6) schedule the next cross-disciplinary design review. Items 4 through 6 must be stated as needed follow-ups without an owner or a due date. Do not assign anyone to them implicitly, do not add dates, and do not resolve who will take them. The meeting should end after the six-item list is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’m looking at the evidence-plan tab, the one with the four retrofit columns. Before we get too far into outcomes and costs, I’d like us to pin down what building information we can actually get without a site visit. The age, roof condition, orientation, and especially service capacity. I was thinking the indoor-heat and load estimates would- otherwise they’re going to be pretty hand-wavy.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Especially service capacity. Maya, what would let us tell an electrical upgrade that's actually required for in-unit cooling apart from one that's more of a precaution? And in these older buildings, is that usually something you can answer at the building level, or can it vary a lot unit by unit?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: It can be both. The service entrance and the main distribution are building-level constraints, but a bad unit panel, shared circuits, or a weak branch circuit can make cooling unusable in just some apartments. I wouldn't call an upgrade required from a nameplate alone. We'd need at least the service rating, panel schedules if they exist, and some estimate of coincident evening use over the hot nights, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: For the health side, I’d want to keep that unit-level uncertainty, not average it away. If cooling is technically installed but a resident can’t safely run it, the relevant exposure is still the overnight indoor temperature, especially for people with limited mobility or cardiopulmonary disease. Maya, can the model show window-opening and actual, actual cooling-use assumptions explicitly, maybe as separate scenarios in that column?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd put those in as explicit cases rather than pretend we know the behavior. Windows open overnight versus closed, and cooling available versus cooling actually operating for, say, the evening and sleep period. The awkward part is that they interact. Opening windows can help on some nights and can make a west-facing unit worse before the outdoor air cools. So we should keep the overnight temperature trace, not just a daily maximum.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: For us, the sleep-period trace is probably the more clinically relevant output. Could we flag, in each scenario, hours above a threshold overnight, not because that gives us attributable emergency visits, it doesn't, but so we can identify buildings where the exposure burden is plausibly concentrated among residents who can't readily leave or use a cooling center?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd keep it as hours above an overnight threshold, and maybe the indoor temperature at dawn too, since that tells us whether the unit actually recovered between days. But I’d be careful not to pick one threshold and treat it like a health prediction. For this first pass, the useful thing is ranking which building-and-retrofit cases stay persistently hot over the whole event.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: For the funding comparison, could that row also say what share of units are actually likely to have usable cooling in each scenario? A building can rank well in the temperature model, but if the electrical constraint leaves, um, the top-floor units out, then the benefits and the tenant bill effects are distributed very differently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can add a usable-cooling share, but it needs to be a range tied to the service and unit-panel information, not a single clean percentage from the model. If we're okay calling it a screening estimate, I can put together the preliminary indoor-temperature and grid-load scope by June 14, 2027. I just don't want it read as calibrated building results before we know which panels and circuits are actually there.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Mm, range is important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: And the range needs a health-facing companion column, not just usable cooling share, but whether the units left out are concentrated on top floors or among residents with limited mobility. I can provide the available aggregate heat-related emergency-visit and cooling-center-use measures, with the suppression and, um, attribution limitations clearly marked, by June 21, 2027. I just can't promise building-level or resident-level linkage.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Before we turn that into dollar figures, I need to check which property and utility-bill fields we can get consistently across candidates. I can draft the comparison framework, owner capital cost alongside likely tenant bill impacts, using ranges for prices and cooling use, by June 18, 2027. I just don't want to- I don't want a single assumed bill increase doing too much work.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d keep Priya’s bill range right next to Maya’s usable-cooling range, instead of treating either one as some secondary implementation note. A resident can have a technically eligible unit and still ration cooling if the operating cost is unacceptable, and from our standpoint, that isn’t the same as protection. I don’t know if the candidate-screening data can tell us anything about mobility or medical vulnerability at that level, though...

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Hm, that’s a real gap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the candidate screen, maybe we don't try to infer medical vulnerability from building records at all. But we can at least flag physical proxies we can verify, like top floor, sun exposure, no elevator, and whether the service information is missing, then Luis can tell us how far that gets us before it becomes misleading.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: Those are useful as exposure proxies, but I'd label them that way, not as vulnerability proxies. No elevator can matter a great deal for someone with impaired mobility, but it doesn't tell us who lives there. And top floor and solar exposure identify thermal risk, not clinical susceptibility. Could the screen have a separate “verification needed” flag for mobility barriers and resident access to cooling alternatives, instead of implying the building record answers that?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd put that in a separate verification flag, not into the thermal score. And for the engineering screen, missing service information should trigger that same kind of flag. Otherwise a building can look retrofit-ready on paper when we really don't know whether units can run cooling through the night.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: From the fund side, that missing-service flag matters for equity too. If we only select buildings with the cleanest records, we could end up favoring owners who already had the staff or money to document everything. Could we keep “information missing” separate from “likely infeasible” so the pilot has a way to do targeted verification instead of quietly screening those properties out?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: For health equity, I’d strongly support keeping those separate. Missing records aren’t evidence of low need, and if targeted verification is the way in, the resident-facing check should ask whether people can realistically use a cooling center, like mobility, transport, and caregiving, instead of trying to infer that from the property file.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works. I’d make targeted verification a distinct middle path in the screen. Records sufficient, records missing and verify, and likely major electrical work. The only thing I’d add is verification has to include at least a look at the service and representative unit panels. Otherwise, we may call a building feasible based on roof and orientation and miss the actual overnight cooling...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd add one small distinction to that middle path. Verifying electrical feasibility is necessary, but that isn't- that's not the resident-access verification. On the screen, maybe use two separate flags, one for service and representative panels, and one for barriers to using either in-unit cooling or a cooling center, so we don't let a technically feasible building read as health-protective by default.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Two flags makes sense. For the service one, I’d also put a minimum evidence line in the sheet, utility or service rating plus a representative panel check, because otherwise “verified” could just mean somebody, somebody found an old listing. And Priya, I still want to know, in the owner material you’ve seen, is service capacity usually known up front, or does it tend to turn up only once they’re already pursuing cooling?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: From the owner interviews, it usually isn't known reliably at the start. A few people could tell me the nominal service rating or what they'd spent on common-area work, but they couldn't say whether representative units could carry overnight cooling. That seemed to come up once a contractor scoped the project. So I'd use owner-reported capacity as a lead for the screen, not as the minimum evidence Maya's describing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Then the sheet shouldn't let an owner report satisfy that field. We can mark it as preliminary only until we have the utility rating and a panel check. Otherwise the model has to carry a pretty wide usable-cooling range. I'm still not sure we can get those records before a visit, so that's something we need to check with the candidate-property intake, and...

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: I’ll check whether intake can consistently supply the property and bill fields for that first screen.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there. I’ll follow up by email once I’ve checked the, um, intake question. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Alvarez
transcript.text: Thank you, Maya and Priya. Take care.
